and he wanted to take [them] and flee to Egypt.
And because I perceived his secret, he gave me poison to drink,
and wanted to kill me.
And if it had not been for this Christian physician named Muwaffaq, from the people of Nisibis, who treated me,
otherwise I would have been dead already.'
And the King of Kings was enraged,
and commanded that they should scourge Bar Yunis.
And while they were stretching him,
a document {amulet/scroll} fell from his bosom.
And they opened it and read it,
and behold, words from their Quran were written in it:
'Let their tongue be bound in their mouth,
and fetters on their feet,
and collars on their necks,
and let us rejoice and exult.'
And when the King of Kings asked,
'What are these words?', the enemies of Bar Yunis answered:
'They are sorceries,
which have been made against you.'
And he commanded, and that Bar Yunis was put to death;
and he set up Zaki of Arbela as ruler in his place.
And he was called by the additional name of 'the Accuser {Slanderer}',
because he had slandered Bar Yunis and killed him.
And in the year one thousand five hundred and seventy-six {1576 AG},
[departed this] world {OCR?} the King of Kings, Hulagu.
For to his wisdom,
and to the greatness of his soul,
and to his wondrous deeds, there was no equal.
And in the days of summer, Doquz Khatun, the believing queen, also departed.
And there was great mourning for the Christians in all the world over the departure of these two great luminaries
and champions of the Christian faith.
After Hulagu, [Abaqa, King of] Kings {OCR?}.
In those days when Hulagu Ilkhan departed from the life of time,
the sons of the kings and the Mongol grandees agreed together
that his eldest son, Abaqa, should sit upon the throne of his father,
because they saw that God had adorned him with reason, wisdom, good will, and mercy.
And when the kingdom was established for him,
he showed himself victorious in all his wars,
and triumphant over all
his enemies,
and he was beloved by all the nations under his rule.
[patriarch] Euthymius. In this very year seventy-six, Euthymius {OCR?}.
